How Much Does a Business Website Cost in the UK? A Practical Guide for Local Businesses

Business website cost in the UK depends on what the website needs to do. A simple brochure site is very different from a website built to capture leads, support SEO, connect forms, automate follow-up, and help the business grow.

By FekitechPublished 6 July 2026Updated 18 July 20268 min read
In this guide
  1. What affects business website cost in the UK?
  2. Simple website vs business-growth website
  3. Website features local businesses should care about
  4. Why cheap websites often become expensive later
  5. What to prepare before contacting a website builder
  6. How Fekitech helps businesses build better digital systems
Software Development / Apps
Quick answer

The practical starting point

Many local business owners ask for a website price before they know what the website should achieve. That makes comparison difficult because two websites can look similar but perform very differently.

A useful business website should help customers trust you, understand your services, make an enquiry, and take the next step. For some businesses, it should also connect to booking, forms, analytics, automation, customer follow-up, or internal workflows.

This guide explains what affects website cost, what features matter, and what to prepare before contacting a website builder.

What affects business website cost in the UK?

Website cost is shaped by scope, content, design quality, technical setup, integrations, SEO needs, and how much strategy is required before build begins.

A small service business may only need a few strong pages and a clear enquiry path. A growing business may need service pages, landing pages, quote forms, booking flows, analytics, CRM handoff, automation, and ongoing improvement.

  • Number of pages and service pages
  • Content writing and page structure
  • Custom design compared with template setup
  • Contact forms, booking, payments, or quote flows
  • SEO setup, metadata, schema, and internal linking
  • Analytics, tracking, and conversion measurement
  • Automation or CRM integration

Simple website vs business-growth website

A simple website tells people who you are and what you offer. A business-growth website is built around trust, search visibility, lead capture, conversion, and operational follow-up.

For a local business, the second option often creates more value because it supports the work behind the enquiry. The website becomes part of the business system, not just a page online.

Website typeTypical focusBest for
Simple brochure websiteBasic pages, contact details, service overviewNew businesses that need a professional online presence
Lead generation websiteService pages, strong CTAs, enquiry forms, SEO basicsLocal businesses that want more enquiries
Business system websiteForms, automation, analytics, booking, CRM handoffGrowing businesses that need the website to save time
Custom web appTailored workflows, portals, dashboards, business logicBusinesses with specific operational problems

Website features local businesses should care about

A good website should make the next step obvious. Visitors should quickly understand what you do, where you work, why they can trust you, and how to contact you.

For many businesses, the highest-value features are not flashy design effects. They are clear service pages, strong calls to action, fast forms, useful content, local SEO structure, and a reliable way to handle enquiries.

  • Clear service pages that match what customers search for
  • Contact forms that ask the right questions
  • Click-to-call and email links
  • Trust signals such as location, process, and real service detail
  • SEO titles and meta descriptions
  • Analytics so you can see what is working
  • Automation for replies, lead routing, or booking

Why cheap websites often become expensive later

A cheap website can be fine if the goal is only to have a small online presence. It becomes expensive when it has to be rebuilt because it cannot support SEO, content growth, forms, automation, or proper conversion tracking.

The real question is not just what the website costs. It is whether the website helps the business get better enquiries, reduce admin, and support the next stage of growth.

What to prepare before contacting a website builder

Before asking for a quote, prepare the basics. You do not need a full technical brief, but you should know what the website needs to achieve for the business.

This makes the conversation clearer and helps the builder recommend the right level of website rather than guessing.

  • Your main services and target customers
  • The locations or markets you serve
  • What action visitors should take
  • Examples of enquiries you want more of
  • Current admin problems around forms, bookings, or follow-up
  • Any systems the website should connect to

That means a website can be planned as part of the wider business system: how enquiries arrive, how they are handled, what gets automated, what gets measured, and how the team follows up.

Common questions

Frequently asked questions

There is no single correct price because scope varies. A basic site, a lead-generation site, and a website with automation or custom software all require different levels of planning, content, design, and development.

Choose the cheapest option only if it still supports your business goal. A low-cost website can become expensive if it needs to be rebuilt for SEO, better forms, analytics, automation, or conversion later.
